los.text: Identify the investigations and treatment strategies underpinning the approach to acute and post-acute stroke disease.
sessions: Clinical evaluation of stroke disease part 2 + investigations
los.html:
PhaseInvestigationsTreatment
Pre-hospitalFAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time to call 999); glucoseRapid transfer to a hyperacute stroke unit; note time last known well
Emergency department
  • Capillary glucose
  • ROSIER score
  • NIHSS (severity)
  • Non-contrast CT head immediately (exclude haemorrhage)
  • CT angiography if thrombectomy possible
  • CT perfusion in selected/late presenters
  • Bloods (FBC, U&E, clotting, glucose, lipids), ECG
See below
Ischaemic: reperfusion
  • Thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) within 4.5 h of onset if haemorrhage excluded and no contraindications (e.g. recent bleeding or surgery, anticoagulation, platelets <100, previous ICH, BP >185/110 not lowered)
  • Mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion (proximal anterior circulation) within 6 h (with thrombolysis if eligible), up to 24 h if imaging shows salvageable brain
  • Posterior circulation (basilar) up to 24 h
Ischaemic: antiplateletAspirin 300 mg daily for 2 weeks once haemorrhage excluded (24 h after thrombolysis), then clopidogrel 75 mg long term
HaemorrhagicReverse anticoagulation (prothrombin complex concentrate + IV vitamin K for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitors), lower BP (systolic target 130–140 mmHg within an hour if presenting early with systolic 150–220), neurosurgery for hydrocephalus or large cerebellar haematoma
Stroke unit care (all)Swallow screen within 4 h before any oral intake
  • Positioning
  • Oxygen only if sats <95%
  • Glucose 4–11 mmol/L
  • Hydration and nutrition (NG tube within 24 h if unsafe swallow)
  • Intermittent pneumatic compression for VTE prevention
  • Early mobilisation
  • Decompressive hemicraniectomy for malignant MCA infarction (within 48 h)
Secondary preventionCarotid Doppler, echo, ambulatory ECG (paroxysmal AF), lipids, HbA1c
  • Clopidogrel
  • Anticoagulation (DOAC) for AF (timing by stroke severity, often within days for minor strokes)
  • High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg)
  • BP control
  • Carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic 50–99% stenosis (within 2 weeks)
  • Stop smoking, alcohol, diet, exercise
  • No driving for 1 month (car)
TIASpecialist assessment within 24 h; MRI (DWI)
  • Aspirin 300 mg immediately
  • Dual antiplatelets (aspirin + clopidogrel for 21 days) after high-risk TIA or minor stroke
  • Then secondary prevention as above
Post-acute
  • MDT rehabilitation (physio, OT, SALT, dietitian, psychology)
  • Early supported discharge
  • Treat complications (aspiration pneumonia, depression, spasticity, shoulder pain, incontinence, falls, pressure ulcers, seizures, fatigue, cognitive problems)
  • 6-month review

los.text: Identify the pathological changes that are associated with intracerebral vascular disease and link to the recognised risk factors for stroke
los.html:
TypePathologyRisk factors / causes
Ischaemic (~85%)
Large artery atherosclerosisPlaque at the carotid bifurcation or intracranial arteries → thrombosis or artery-to-artery embolismHypertension, smoking, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes
CardioembolicThrombus in the left atrial appendage (AF), after MI (LV thrombus), endocarditis, prosthetic valves, paradoxical embolism (PFO)AF, heart disease
Small vessel (lacunar)Lipohyalinosis/microatheroma of deep penetrating arteries → small deep infarcts (internal capsule, thalamus, pons)Hypertension, diabetes
OtherArterial dissection (young, neck pain, Horner's), vasculitis, thrombophilia, sickle cell, cocaine
Haemorrhagic (~15%)
Intracerebral haemorrhage
  • Rupture of small deep perforators damaged by hypertension (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum)
  • Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (lobar haemorrhage in older people)
  • AVMs, tumours
Hypertension, anticoagulants, alcohol, cocaine
Subarachnoid haemorrhageRupture of a berry aneurysm at the circle of WillisSmoking, hypertension, ADPKD, connective tissue disease, family history
Ischaemic cascade
  • Occlusion
  • → core (irreversible infarction) surrounded by the penumbra (stunned but salvageable)
  • → energy failure, glutamate excitotoxicity, Ca²⁺ influx, free radicals, cytotoxic oedema
  • → necrosis (liquefactive, leaving a cavity)
  • "time is brain" (millions of neurons lost per minute), the basis of rapid reperfusion
  • Haemorrhagic transformation can follow.
Risk factors
  • Non-modifiable: age, male sex, ethnicity (Black and South Asian), family history, previous stroke/TIA
  • Modifiable: hypertension (the biggest), AF, smoking, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, obesity, inactivity, alcohol, salt, carotid stenosis, sleep apnoea, drugs (cocaine).

los.text: Identify the relevant history and examination appropriate to a patient with an acute cerebrovascular event.
sessions: Clinical evaluation of stroke disease part 1
los.html:
• History:
AskWhy
Exact time of onset / last known wellThrombolysis and thrombectomy windows (wake-up strokes: last seen well)
Symptoms: sudden weakness, numbness, facial droop, speech or language disturbance, visual loss, diplopia, vertigo, ataxia, swallowing problemsLocalisation
Headache, vomiting, reduced consciousnessHaemorrhage, raised ICP, posterior circulation
Neck painDissection
Seizure at onsetTodd's paresis (mimic)
Previous TIA/stroke; AF, hypertension, diabetes, smokingRisk and cause
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets, recent surgery, bleeding, head injuryBleeding risk, thrombolysis contraindications
Pre-stroke function (modified Rankin)Treatment decisions, rehabilitation goals
Stroke mimicsHypoglycaemia, seizure/Todd's paresis, migraine with aura, sepsis/delirium, functional disorder, tumour, subdural haematoma, MS, Bell's palsy, syncope.
Examination
  • ABCDE, glucose, BP, pulse (AF), temperature, GCS
  • NIHSS
  • Cranial nerves (visual fields, gaze, UMN facial weakness)
  • Limbs (tone and reflexes may be reduced acutely, then increase)
  • Plantars
  • Coordination
  • Sensation
  • Speech (dysphasia vs dysarthria)
  • Neglect
  • Heart murmurs, carotid bruits
  • Swallow screen.
Oxford (Bamford) classFeatures
TACS (total anterior circulation)All three: unilateral weakness/sensory loss (≥2 of face, arm, leg), homonymous hemianopia, higher cortical dysfunction (dysphasia, neglect)
PACS (partial anterior)Two of three, or higher cortical dysfunction alone
LACS (lacunar)Pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, or ataxic hemiparesis; no cortical signs or field defect
POCS (posterior circulation)Cerebellar or brainstem signs, isolated homonymous hemianopia, cranial nerve palsy with contralateral limb signs, bilateral signs
TerritoryDeficit
ACAContralateral leg > arm weakness, behavioural change, urinary incontinence
MCAContralateral face and arm > leg weakness and sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant)
PCAContralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Lateral medulla (PICA, Wallenberg)Ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, Horner's, ataxia, dysphagia; contralateral body pain/temperature loss
Midbrain (Weber's)Ipsilateral III palsy, contralateral hemiparesis

los.text: Identify the investigations and treatment strategies that underpin the current approach to acute and post-acute stroke disease
sessions: Investigation and management of cerebrovascular disease
los.html:
• Evidence behind the pathway:
StrategyEvidence
Organised stroke unit careReduces death and dependency for all stroke types: the single most important intervention
Thrombolysis
  • More patients independent at 3–6 months despite a small risk of symptomatic ICH
  • Benefit greatest the earlier it's given (within 4.5 h)
Mechanical thrombectomy
  • Very effective for large vessel occlusion (about 1 in 3 treated gain functional independence)
  • Extended to 24 h with perfusion selection
Aspirin within 48 hSmall but definite reduction in recurrence and death
Short-term dual antiplateletFewer recurrences after minor stroke/high-risk TIA (more bleeding if prolonged)
Anticoagulation for AF~2/3 relative reduction in stroke; DOACs have less intracranial haemorrhage than warfarin
Statins, BP loweringReduce recurrence
Carotid endarterectomyLarge benefit for symptomatic 70–99% stenosis, some for 50–69%, greatest if done early
Decompressive hemicraniectomyImproves survival in malignant MCA infarction
Intermittent pneumatic compressionReduces DVT and may improve survival (stockings don't help)
Imaging choices
  • Non-contrast CT first (fast, excludes haemorrhage, which is hyperdense immediately)
  • CT angiography (vessel occlusion, carotids)
  • CT perfusion or MRI DWI (core vs penumbra, wake-up strokes, TIA)
  • Carotid Doppler (stenosis).
Post-acute strategyEarly MDT rehabilitation, early supported discharge, secondary prevention, return to driving and work advice, long-term follow-up (mood, cognition, spasticity, carers).

los.text: Identify the major tracts of the brainstem in transverse section.
los.html:
LevelFront (ventral)MiddleBack (dorsal)
Midbrain (superior colliculus)Cerebral peduncles (corticospinal and corticobulbar), substantia nigra, CN III nucleus and fibres, red nucleusMedial lemniscus, spinothalamic tract (lateral)Cerebral aqueduct, periaqueductal grey, superior colliculi
PonsBasilar pons: corticospinal fibres broken up by pontine nuclei; transverse pontocerebellar fibresMedial lemniscus (now horizontal), spinothalamic, MLF, VI and VII nuclei4th ventricle floor
Medulla (open, upper)Pyramids (corticospinal), inferior oliveMedial lemniscus (vertical, beside the midline), spinothalamic (lateral), XII nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract4th ventricle, vagal nuclei, nucleus solitarius
Medulla (closed, lower)Pyramidal decussationSpinothalamic, spinal trigeminalGracile and cuneate nuclei and fasciculi; sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibres)
  • MLF (medial longitudinal fasciculus) links III, IV and VI nuclei: damage (MS) → internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
  • Rule of 4s for brainstem syndromes: 4 midline structures start with M (motor tract, medial lemniscus, MLF, motor nuclei III, IV, VI, XII)
    • 4 lateral ones with S (spinocerebellar, spinothalamic, sensory V nucleus, sympathetic).

los.text: Identify the pathway of the corticospinal tract from the pre-central gyrus to the anterior horn cell and link to the functional consequences of damage at different points along that pathway.
los.html:
1Precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex, Betz cells; leg medially, face laterally).
2. Corona radiataPosterior limb of the internal capsule.
3. Cerebral peduncle(midbrain)Basilar pons → medullary pyramid.
4. Pyramidal decussation(~85–90% cross)Lateral corticospinal tract (the rest: anterior corticospinal tract, cross at their level).
5Synapse on the anterior horn cell (lower motor neuron) → muscle.
Lesion siteEffect
Motor cortex (e.g. MCA stroke)Contralateral weakness of face and arm more than leg (ACA: leg)
Internal capsule (lacunar)Dense contralateral hemiplegia (face, arm, leg equally)
BrainstemContralateral hemiplegia + ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy (crossed signs, e.g. Weber's)
Spinal cord (above the anterior horn)Ipsilateral UMN weakness below the lesion
Anterior horn / nerveLMN signs at that level
UMN signsLMN signs
Spasticity (clasp-knife), hyperreflexia, upgoing plantar (Babinski), clonus, no wasting early, pyramidal pattern (extensors weak in arms, flexors in legs)Flaccid, hyporeflexia, wasting, fasciculations, downgoing plantar

los.text: Identify the routes of the two principal sensory pathways from the dorsal root ganglion to the thalamus and parietal lobe and link to the functional consequences of damage at different points along that pathway.
los.html:
Dorsal column–medial lemniscusSpinothalamic (anterolateral)
ModalitiesFine touch, vibration, proprioceptionPain, temperature, crude touch
1st neuronDRG → up the dorsal column on the same side (gracile: legs, medial; cuneate: arms, lateral)DRG → synapse in the dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa)
CrossesMedulla (internal arcuate fibres) after synapsing in the gracile/cuneate nucleiSpinal cord, within 1–2 segments (anterior white commissure)
2nd neuronMedial lemniscus → thalamusSpinothalamic tract → thalamus
3rd neuronVPL → postcentral gyrus (parietal lobe)VPL → postcentral gyrus
Lesion siteEffect
Hemisection (Brown-Séquard)Same side: proprioception/vibration loss and weakness; opposite side: pain and temperature loss (from 1–2 levels below)
Central cord (syringomyelia)Cape-like bilateral pain and temperature loss (crossing fibres); dorsal columns spared
Dorsal columns (B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis)Lost vibration and proprioception; sensory ataxia, positive Romberg's
Anterior spinal arteryWeakness and pain/temperature loss; dorsal columns spared
Above the medulla (brainstem, thalamus, cortex)All sensation lost on the opposite side
ThalamusContralateral loss; thalamic pain syndrome
Parietal cortexContralateral loss of fine discrimination (astereognosis, two-point), neglect (non-dominant)

los.text: Recognise the normal brainstem and cerebellum, and common pathology on radiological images.
los.html:
ImagingNormal featuresCommon pathology
CT (first in acute stroke, trauma)
  • Brainstem and cerebellum in the posterior fossa
  • 4th ventricle (CSF dark) in front of the cerebellum
  • Streak artefact from the petrous bones limits detail
Cerebellar haemorrhage (bright: surgical emergency if >3 cm or hydrocephalus); infarct (dark, often missed early on CT); hydrocephalus (dilated ventricles)
MRI (best for the posterior fossa)Midbrain (peduncles, aqueduct), pons (bulging basilar part), medulla (pyramids, olives); cerebellar hemispheres, vermis, folia; tonsils above the foramen magnum
  • Posterior circulation stroke (bright on diffusion-weighted imaging)
  • MS plaques
  • Vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle
  • Chiari malformation (tonsils >5 mm below foramen magnum)
  • Tumours (medulloblastoma in children, metastases, haemangioblastoma)
  • Warning sign: a swollen cerebellum (infarct or bleed) compresses the 4th ventricle (obstructive hydrocephalus) and the brainstem (coning).
